Abstract
The rapid growth of cloud computing has brought scalability and flexibility to modern organizations, but it has 
also introduced a new wave of complex and evolving security threats. Traditional security mechanisms, such as 
static rule-based systems and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), often fall short of identifying advanced attacks like 
insider threats, privilege escalation, and data breaches. Addressing this gap, we propose SmartTrust, a hybrid deep 
learning framework designed for real-time threat detection in cloud environments built on Zero-Trust Architecture 
(ZTA) principles. SmartTrust integrates CNN, LSTM, and Transformer models to analyze spatial and temporal patterns 
in network traffic and user behaviours. Unlike conventional models, it leverages Reinforcement Learning to enable 
adaptive decision-making, allowing it to adjust responses based on real-time contextual signals dynamically. To 
ensure transparency and tamper-proof event tracking, the framework also incorporates blockchain-based logging 
that is aligned with ZTA compliance. We evaluated SmartTrust on two benchmark datasets, CIC-IoT 2023 and 
UNSW-NB15, which simulate realistic cloud-based attack scenarios. The model achieved detection rates of 99.19% 
for insider threats, 98.23% for privilege escalation, and 99.27% for data breaches while reducing false positives by 
over 40% compared to existing approaches. Though the model’s complexity introduces higher computational 
demands, its performance demonstrates that SmartTrust offers a robust, intelligent, and adaptive alternative to 
traditional cloud security solutions capable of evolving with today’s rapidly changing threat landscape.

Introduction
Cloud computing has transformed how organizations 
manage and process data, offering scalability and flex­
ibility. However, this has introduced new and com­
plex security challenges, as traditional security models 
struggle to defend against advanced, evolving threats 
like insider attacks and privilege escalation. SmartTrust 
addresses these issues by integrating Zero-Trust Archi­
tecture (ZTA) with advanced deep learning models, 
providing real-time, adaptive threat detection in cloud 
environments.
Background
Cloud computing changed the ways in which how orga­
nizations have been storing, managing and processing 
data and cloud computing solutions are scalable and 
cost-effective solutions for many business operations. It 
has gained immense popularity over last few years owing 
to its ability to provide flexible infrastructure, on-demand 
resources, and global connectivity [1]. Cloud platforms 
are used by organizations of all sizes to reduce capex, 
improve operational agility and accelerate innovation. 
Although there are many advantages in using cloud com­
puting, it offers a new comprehensive set of challenges 
that require to be reduce to ensure secure and reliable 
services [2].
The most critical issue when it comes to the cloud is 
security. Today, organizations migrating their most 
critical data and applications into the cloud face numer­
ous security challenges, ranging from data leaks, and 
unauthorized access, to service interruptions. Cloud 
environments employ shared resources, multi-tenant 
architectures, and dynamic workloads [2] that signifi­
cantly increase their attack surface compared to tradi­
tional on-premise infrastructures, making their security 
approach based on security measures extending well 
beyond the perimeter and beyond static access controls 
[3, 4]. Cloud computing emphasizes security. Cloud 
infrastructure may also come under severe assault, which 
could spell disaster in the form of losses, reputation dam­
age, liability claims, and workflow interruption. The effect 
is significant for sectors handling sensitive information 
such as healthcare, finance, and government. This trend 
toward sophistication is further exacerbated by emerg­
ing attack vectors, including advanced persistent threats 
(APTs), zero-day exploits, and insider threats illustrating 
the cloud security challenges [5, 6].
Insider threats and privilege escalation are two of the 
worst and equally complex problems of cloud security. A 
wide range of legitimate users (such as employees, con­
tractors, or business partners) misuses their access to sys­
tem information either maliciously or inadvertently, and 
these threats are called insider threats. One notable case, 
centred on a global financial services giant, saw an insider 
covertly exfiltrate sensitive customer data for months, 
avoiding detection while costing the company millions in 
lost revenue and a tarnished reputation. Privilege escala­
tion attacks target the vulnerabilities exposed by miscon­
figurations in the cloud, or the software itself, enabling 
the attacker to gain unauthorized elevated access rights 
(at least on the application level) which can lead to the 
complete system being compromised/or even the entire 
cloud infrastructure, in some cases. These attacks are 
the most sinister as they mimic regular network traf­
fic, which makes it next to impossible for traditional 
perimeter defenses and/or static access controls to work 
against them. These emerging threat scenarios highlight 
the importance of intelligent, contextual, and adaptive 
security solutions that utilize the real-time behavioural 
analytics to detect and defend against these hidden per­
sistence threats.
In order to mitigate these risks, organizations need 
to implement comprehensive and adaptable security 
architectures that can be context aware and responsive 
to real-time threats. In this context, a pragmatic solu­
tion is appearing: the ZTA. ZTA is based on the tenet of 
never trust, always verify, meaning no application, user 
or device is granted implicit trust, whether it is located 
within or outside the network perimeter. It means that 
each request for access is scrutinized and is granted only 
if after a long verification process. ZTA strengthens cloud 
security while minimizing the risk of unauthorized access 
by continually evaluating access requests using contex­
tual information like user behaviour, device health, and 
access patterns. But while ZTA strengthens access con­
trol and reduces the attack surface, It May not be Enough 
to Address the full scope of Next-Gen Cyber Threats 
[7–10]. The use of advanced machine learning techniques 
as part of a continuous delivery process is necessary for 
ZTA to improve, and to secure the cloud with a better 
defense mechanism.
Challenges in existing cloud security models
Even though cloud security has come a long way, cur­
rent models often rely too much on static defenses and 
reactive threat detection systems. Examples of traditional 
security systems include firewalls, IDS, and access con­
trol lists (ACLs). They are meant to find known attack 
signatures and enforce rules already set. However, these 
methods are becoming less effective against sophisticated 
cyber threats that change quickly and take advantage of 
zero-day vulnerabilities [5, 11–13]. One big problem with 
how cloud security is set up now is that it relies on detec­
tion after the fact. MFA is a good way to ensure users are 
who they say they are, but it doesn’t offer much protec­
tion once access is granted. This leaves a security hole 
because bad authenticate people can exploit system flaws, 
gain more access, and steal sensitive data without setting

Another problem is that hybrid and multi-cloud

Insider threats are also becoming a more significant 
problem for cloud security. On the other hand, insider 
threats come from people who have permission to access 
cloud resources, like employees, contractors, or business 
partners, and may do so maliciously or accidentally. You 
need more than just fixed rules to find and stop insider 
threats. You need adaptive, behaviour-based analytics to 
spot strange activities in real-time. These problems make 
it clear that cloud security must be more flexible and 
intelligent. It must use advanced deep learning models, 
contextual data analysis, and constant adaptation to find 
and stop threats as they appear [2, 16].
Research questions
The research presented in this paper addresses the fol­
lowing key questions.
 	•
How can a hybrid deep learning framework enhance 
real-time threat detection in dynamic cloud 
environments?
 	•
What advantages does the integration of Zero-Trust 
Architecture with machine learning models offer 
over conventional cloud security strategies?
 	•
How can reinforcement learning improve the 
adaptability and accuracy of cloud security systems 
in identifying and mitigating insider threats, privilege 
escalation, and multi-stage cyberattacks?
 	•
What are the comparative performance metrics of 
a hybrid LSTM-CNN-Transformer model versus 
independent deep learning models in identifying 
cloud-based security threats?
 	•
How can blockchain-based logging guarantee 
transparency, integrity, and non-repudiation of 
security incidents within cloud environments?
This investigation seeks to address these research ques­
tions and deliver a comprehensive and adaptive security 
solution that protects cloud infrastructure from complex 
and evolving cyber threats.
Research motivations
The growing dependence on cloud computing has 
heightened the complexity of cyber threats targeting 
cloud environments. Traditional security measures, such 
as MFA and static defenses, are frequently ineffective 
against emerging attack vectors such as insider threats, 
privilege escalation, and data breaches. These constraints 
highlight the need for more dynamic, proactive security 
solutions that quickly adapt to emerging threats [14, 17]. 
Contemporary security systems frequently fail to detect 
complex patterns in network traffic and user behaviour, 
resulting in delayed or inadequate responses to breaches.
Furthermore, static defenses fail to consider the con­
text of user access, such as device status or access tim­
ing, which can significantly impact threat detection 
accuracy. As a result, the challenge is to develop a secu­
rity framework capable of detecting advanced threats 
while continuously learning, adapting, and prioritizing 
high-risk activities in real time. The SmartTrust Frame­
work addresses these challenges by combining ZTA with 
advanced deep learning models and RL, allowing for pro­
active threat detection, immediate response, and con­
text-aware security measures. The framework provides 
an innovative solution for addressing emerging security 
challenges in cloud environments by combining LSTM 
networks, hybrid neural networks, and AI-driven risk 
assessment [5, 18].

vide a dynamic and highly effective security solution, 
establishing a new standard for cloud protection against 
today’s complex threats. The SmartTrust Framework 
introduces a new approach to cloud security with the fol­
lowing key contributions, offering a fresh perspective and 
innovative solutions to security challenges.
 	•
Introduction of SmartTrust Framework: Combining 
ZTA with many innovative deep learning models, the 
proposed SmartTrust Framework is a modern cloud 
security solution. These models call for Transformer 
networks, CNNs, and LSTM networks. This hybrid 
approach makes it feasible to identify complicated 
cyber threats in real-time and with adaptive 
capabilities [12].
 	•
Context-Sensitive Security: Unlike conventional 
security systems, SmartTrust dynamically responds 
to real-time changes in user behaviour, access 
patterns, and device status. The framework 
constantly improves its defense mechanisms through 
reinforcement Learning, lowering false positives, and 
raising general detection accuracy [13].
 	•
Comprehensive Threat Detection: With high accuracy 
rates of 99.19%, 98.23%, and 99.27%, respectively,

Related works
This section on related work examines current research 
on cloud security, the use of machine learning, and 
sophisticated methods designed to improve system integ­
rity. Diverse methodologies, including deep learning 
models, federated learning, and Zero Trust frameworks, 
have been proposed to address the challenges of secur­
ing cloud environments and IoT networks. These studies 
highlight the ongoing progress in threat detection and 
mitigation strategies, providing a foundation for further 
improvements in real-time security solutions.
Cloud security and deep learning techniques
Hazman et al. [1] investigated using LSTM and XGBoost 
models to improve the security of IoT-enabled smart cit­
ies. The study emphasizes using deep learning techniques 
to detect security breaches in smart cities. The authors 
present a novel hybrid model for real-time threat detec­
tion that combines LSTM for sequential data analysis and 
XGBoost for classification tasks. The model was evalu­
ated using IoT datasets and exhibited enhanced detec­
tion accuracy relative to conventional methods. The 
study recognizes the need for additional optimization to 
manage IoT data’s extensive and varied characteristics 
in smart cities. Alotaibi et al. [2] examine the applica­
tion of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for clas­
sifying web phishing within secure IoT systems. Their 
research underscores the necessity for transparent and 
interpretable machine learning models that aid cyberse­
curity experts in comprehending phishing attempts. The 
authors employ XAI techniques to develop an intuitive 
model that classifies phishing URLs in real time, thereby 
augmenting the security of cloud-based cyber-physical 
systems. One key finding is that explainability improves 
detection and trust in AI-generated decisions. Nonethe­
less, the constraints include maintaining high accuracy 
while ensuring complete transparency.
Mallidi and Ramisetty [5] thoroughly analyze AI-
driven IDS advancements for IoT environments. The 
authors demonstrate multiple deep learning models and 
their efficacy in various IoT applications, emphasizing 
the benefits of CNNs, RNNs, and GANs in identifying 
security threats. The authors claim that AI techniques 
can significantly reduce false positives and improve the 
detection speed of IDSs. Still, they also highlight the sig­
nificant computational costs associated with implement­
ing these models in resource-limited IoT devices. Bensaid 
et al. [11] describe a federated learning-based approach 
to intrusion detection in fog-assisted IoT smart homes. 
Their approach ensures data privacy through decentral­
ized learning, which is critical in contexts involving the 
exchange of sensitive information. The study emphasizes 
using federated learning to reduce network overhead 
while maintaining high detection efficacy. Notwithstand­
ing the encouraging outcomes, the paper indicates that 
issues concerning model convergence and heterogeneous 
data sources in IoT networks remain unresolved.
Kim and Song [12] concentrate on identifying anoma­
lous behaviours through deep learning within zero-trust 
security frameworks. They employ deep learning meth­
odologies, specifically CNNs, to detect anomalies in stan­
dard behaviors within a zero-trust framework, wherein 
no entity is automatically deemed trustworthy. The 
findings indicate that the model proficiently identifies

Machine learning and IoT security
Barach et al. [13] present a multi-layered defense strategy 
for achieving Zero Trust Security in Software Defined 
Networks (SDNs). The paper focuses on using machine 
learning models to detect and respond to security 
breaches in SDN environments. The author contends that 
SDNs benefit from AI-driven solutions because of their 
flexibility and dynamic configuration. The outcome is a 
comprehensive framework that can handle new vulner­
abilities as they appear. Its main drawback is the study’s 
reliance on high-quality data for efficient model training, 
a resource that might not always be consistently available 
in real-world situations. Nawshin et al. [14] use Differen­
tial Privacy and Zero Trust Security concepts to detect 
malware in IoT networks. Their model uses differential 
privacy techniques to protect IoT devices from cyberat­
tacks while maintaining user privacy. Differential privacy 
and artificial intelligence protect personal information 
and detect malware. However, the study discovered that 
real-time implementation still challenges balancing pri­
vacy and detection accuracy.
Kishore et al. [15] present a predictive trust model for 
high-performance blockchain networks that employs 
VARMA, GRU, and LSTM methodologies. Their 
research aims to improve trust prediction by combining 
time-series analysis and deep learning to produce more 
accurate trust assessments in blockchain transactions. 
The proposed model improves precision in recogniz­
ing trustworthy entities in a blockchain context. A noted 
limitation is the complexity and computational require­
ments of training such a hybrid model, which may limit 
its applicability in smaller blockchain systems. Cheruku 
and Narasimha [6] investigate anomaly detection in 
identity and access management (IAM) systems with 
1D-SCNNs. This model detects identity fraud and unau­
thorised access in IAM systems by analyzing sequen­
tial user behaviours. The model performs exceptionally 
well in anomaly detection, with a low false positive rate. 
Nonetheless, one challenge is the complexity of optimiz­
ing the network to balance performance and computa­
tional efficiency.
With an emphasis on Internet of Medical Things 
(IoMT) devices, Khan et al. [16] examine the applica­
tion of deep learning for anomaly detection in intelligent 
healthcare systems. Their results demonstrate that deep 
learning techniques, like LSTMs, can identify abnor­
mal patient behaviors or broken equipment, enhanc­
ing the general security and reliability of healthcare 
IoT networks. Even though the model correctly detects 
anomalies, the authors note that the methodology neces­
sitates extensive datasets for training, which aren’t always 
accessible in the healthcare industry.
Advanced security and privacy solutions in cloud 
computing
Ni and Li [19] investigate the challenges and solutions 
to industrial IoT (IIoT) security, focusing on machine 
learning’s role in threat detection and mitigation. Their 
research focuses on securing industrial IoT networks 
with machine learning algorithms like decision trees 
and SVMs. They conclude that these methods can sig­
nificantly improve real-time threat detection in IIoT sys­
tems. However, the limitations stem from the models’ 
ability to scale when dealing with large IIoT devices pro­
ducing massive amounts of data.
Bobelin et al. [20] delineate the creation of a security-
conscious cloud architecture designed to enhance cloud 
security while preserving optimal performance. The 
authors propose a thorough framework for integrat­
ing various security methodologies in cloud computing 
environments, such as encryption and access control. 
This methodology aims to lessen the likelihood of data 
breaches and access by unauthorized parties. Neverthe­
less, the research acknowledges that achieving a balance 
between performance and security remains a significant 
challenge, particularly in cloud environments that experi­
ence a high volume of traffic.
Sundar et al. [21] present an enhanced cloud security 
framework. This framework uses the Quantum Key Dis­
tribution Protocol (QKDP) to improve data protection. 
Incorporating quantum cryptography into the model 
ensures that data confidentiality is maintained through­
out the cloud computing process, including storage and 
transmission. In addition, it has been demonstrated that 
combining quantum encryption with traditional security 
protocols increases data confidentiality. Nevertheless, the 
authors emphasize that quantum encryption is still in 
the experimental phase, which indicates that additional 
research is required before it can be implemented on a 
significantly larger scale.
Zarichuk et al. [4] investigate ways to maintain privacy 
and ensure integration within cloud computing applica­
tions, focusing on sensitive data protection throughout 
migration. The paper proposes several privacy-preserving 
techniques for user data during transmission, including 
homomorphic encryption and multi-party computation. 
Although the findings are positive, the paper notes that 
these methods have a high computational overhead,

Dataset
This study uses two significant datasets to evaluate the 
effectiveness of the proposed SmartTrust Framework 
in cloud security.
 	•
CIC IoT Dataset 2023: This study uses the CIC 
IoT Dataset 2023, which is one of the most highly 
realistic IoT network environments to date and 
the most comprehensive dataset for testing 
and evaluating cloud security frameworks. The 
Cybersecurity dataset is composed of data captured 
through 105 real IoT devices and is capable to 
document 33 attack types perpetrated by malicious 
IoT devices, compiled by the Canadian Institute 
for Cybersecurity (CIC). They cover seven major 
categories of attacks DDoS, DoS, Reconnaissance, 
Web-based attacks, Brute Force, Spoofing & Mirai 
botnet activities. There are 46 features and one label 
in the dataset with primary features including types 
of protocols used, count of records with success 
and failure flags and rates of traffic that helps find 
anomalies in the network data. It is being segregated 
in to folders holds the raw Packet capture (PCAPs) 
files and feature extract CSV files for machine 
learning exercises [7, 22].
The CIC IoT Dataset 2023 was selected due to its capac­
ity to realistically mimic the characteristics of the IoT 
network traffic and various attack types that can be found 
in practical scenarios, thereby, ensuring an effective envi­
ronment for testing the threat detection potentials of the 
SmartTrust framework. Furthermore, the presence of 
multiple attack vectors over a large set of devices makes 
the results of our experiments more applicable to real­
istic cloud-IoT security settings. Nonetheless, it worths 
to mention some limitations: the dataset is captured in 
a controlled environment that could not entirely reflect 
the different behaviours of traffic, along with new zero-
day attacks, in actual networks. And advanced persis­
tent threats (APTs), so-called highly sophisticated and 
persistent threats, are not represented at the same lev­
els. Finally, in order to overcome valuable content loss of 
data, in addition to CIC IoT data, the UNSW-NB15 data­
set is also used for this study to cover wider evaluation 
and make the model more robust. The attack numbers

Proposed hybrid framework
The SmartTrust Framework combines ZTA with 
advanced deep learning models, including LSTM net­
works and Hybrid Neural Networks, to detect cyber 
threats in cloud environments. We also propose a hybrid 
model architecture that aligns with the framework’s 
capabilities by considering its design and the integration 
of AI-driven risk assessment, reinforcement learning, 
and real-time anomaly detection [2, 6]. Figure 1 presents 
the architecture of the Proposed SmartTrust Framework.
Working of proposed hybrid model
The complete working of the proposed hybrid model is 
as follows.
Data pre-processing layer
The Data Pre-processing Layer is essential to the deep learn­
ing pipeline because it ensures the model adequately prepares 
raw input data for training, testing, and real-time inference 
[16]. The quality and organization of input data significantly 
impact the effectiveness of deep learning models. Efficient 
preprocessing increases model accuracy and decreases the 
likelihood of overfitting, allowing for better generalization of 
new data. Within the SmartTrust Framework, the data pre-
processing layer converts raw network traffic, user behavior 
logs, and contextual information into functional features for 
deep learning models such as Zero-Trust and hybrid archi­
tectures like LSTM, CNN, and Transformer. This phase 
includes normalization, feature extraction, sequence format­
ting, and categorical variable encoding [19, 23]. Algorithm 1 
and Fig. 2 present the architecture of the Data pre-processing 
layer. The detailed process is as follows.
Data cleaning 
 	•
CIC IoT 2023: The dataset includes traffic logs 
from over 105 IoT devices. Some CSV file records 
contain missing or incorrect entries, particularly 
flag values or protocol identifiers. After removing 
records with more than 30% missing values, we used 
mean imputation to impute the remaining missing 
numerical values. Pandas-based filters, such as NaN 
strings, were used to clean up.
 	•
UNSW-NB15: Generated in a controlled testbed, 
this dataset had fewer missing values. Minor gaps in 
categorical columns like “service” were filled using 
mode imputation, while outliers in packet size and 
flow duration were filtered using the Z-score method 
(threshold = ± 3).

Zero-Trust Verification Layer
The Zero-Trust Verification Layer is an essential ele­
ment in the suggested hybrid model. This layer executes 
the Zero Trust Architecture, adhering to the principle of 
“never trust, always verify.” It guarantees that no entity 
is inherently trusted, regardless of its location within or 
outside the network [24]. Every access request is per­
petually authenticated and authorized before system 
interaction. This method improves security by mitigat­
ing the risk of insider threats, privilege escalation, and 
unauthorized access to sensitive assets. The Zero-Trust 
Verification Layer is intricately connected with deep 
learning models (LSTM, Transformer) and the reinforce­
ment learning component, perpetually adjusting security 
policies according to observed behaviors, access patterns, 
and real-time anomaly detection. Figure 3 presents the 
architecture of ZTA.
Key components of ZTA  The key components of ZTA 
are as follows [20, 25].
 	•
Identity and Access Management (IAM): Each 
individual and device is authenticated, and access 
privileges are constantly checked. The identities of 
users, devices, and services are verified using various 
attributes.
 	•
Contextual Access Control: In the Zero-Trust model, 
access decisions are based on multiple factors, such 
as:
◦ User Identity: Verifying user credentials, roles, and 
permissions.
◦ Device Health: Checking the security status of the 
device (e.g., patching, antivirus, etc.) [2, 3, 5].
◦ Time and Location: Access is adjusted based on the 
time of access and geographic location.
◦ Behavioural Context: User and system behaviors 
are continuously monitored, and deviations are 
flagged.
 	•
Continuous Authentication: In conventional security 
models, authentication occurs only once, such as 
when you log in. However, in ZTA, authentication 
occurs continuously. Every new action or attempt to 
gain access is checked in real-time [3, 13].

negatives), or system inefficiencies. The Q-values are 
revised through temporal-difference learning to inform

Hyperparameter tuning
In our research, we focused on fine-tuning the Smart­
Trust Framework’s hyperparameters to improve the 
performance of our deep-learning models for threat 
detection. The learning rate, batch size, number of 
epochs, and optimizer were the most significant hyper­
parameters we altered. We wanted to find the optimal 
configuration to allow the model to learn without over­
fitting or underfitting [32]. A systematic hyperparam­
eter tuning approach utilizing grid search and stratified 
k-fold cross-validation was implemented to enhance the 
performance of the deep learning models in the Smart­
Trust Framework. Grid search was used to investigate a 
specified hyperparameter space for each model architec­
ture, encompassing LSTM, CNN, and Transformer net­
works. Parameters for LSTM, including the number of 
units (64, 128, 256), dropout rates (0.2, 0.4, 0.5), learning

els were calibrated concerning filter sizes, kernel dimen­
sions, pooling layers, and learning rates. In contrast, 
Transformer models were refined according to the num­
ber of attention heads, layers, hidden dimensions, and 
feed-forward network sizes. These combinations were 
thoroughly evaluated to determine the configuration that 
produced the highest F1 score on the validation sets [2].
To ensure a rigorous and impartial assessment dur­
ing tuning, we employed Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Valida­
tion, which preserves uniform class distribution across 
all folds—essential for imbalanced datasets such as 
UNSW-NB15. The dataset was divided in each fold so 
that 80% was allocated for training and 20% for valida­
tion, maintaining class proportions. Performance metrics 
such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-
ROC were calculated for each hyperparameter configu­
ration, and the model with the highest average F1 score 
across the folds was chosen for final deployment. This 
meticulous tuning strategy enhanced model generaliza­
tion and guaranteed equitable performance assessment 
across all classes, including minority attack categories 
[29].

Conclusion and future directions
Conclusions
Cloud computing has revolutionized organizational 
data management and accessibility, concurrently pre­
senting more sophisticated cyber threats. This study 
presents SmartTrust, a real-time, intelligent threat 
detection framework designed to secure modern cloud 
environments. SmartTrust utilizes hybrid deep learn­
ing models specifically CNNs, LSTMs, and Transformer 
networks combined with ZTA and Reinforcement Learn­
ing—to continuously monitor network traffic and user 
behavior, thus detecting complex attack patterns such as 
insider threats, privilege escalation, and data breaches. 
Unlike traditional security systems that rely on static 
rules or mechanisms such as Multi-Factor Authentica­
tion, SmartTrust adapts dynamically based on contex­
tual elements, including access behavior, device integrity, 
and user activity. It employs blockchain-based logging 
to ensure auditability, immutability, and transparency in 
all security events, reinforcing adherence to Zero-Trust 
principles.
We evaluated SmartTrust using two comprehensive 
benchmark datasets, CIC IoT 2023 and UNSW-NB15, 
which simulate real-world cloud-based attacks. The 
results were auspicious: SmartTrust detected 99.19% of 
insider threats, 98.23% of privilege escalation attempts, 
and 99.27% of data breaches while reducing false posi­
tives by over 40% compared to baseline models, including 
CNN, Transformer-CNN, and LSTM-CNN hybrids. Not­
withstanding SmartTrust’s strong performance, specific 
limitations remain. The model demonstrates increased

Future directions
The SmartTrust framework has shown considerable 
efficacy in real-time threat detection and adaptive 
response in cloud environments; however, there are mul­
tiple opportunities for further research and development. 
Extending SmartTrust’s threat detection capabilities to 
include more complex and persistent attack vectors, such 
as multi-stage attacks and Advanced Persistent Threats 
(APTs), represents a crucial area for future research. Such 
attacks are generally defined by their stealth, persistence, 
and adaptability, which complicates detection through 
conventional methods. Future versions of SmartTrust 
will enhance the identification of sophisticated threats by 
integrating augmented behavioral modeling, adversarial 
learning, and context-aware profiling.
Secondly, maintaining a strong emphasis on scalability 
in large and busy cloud environments remains essential. 
Future development should explore a microservices-
based architecture, where different parts of the frame­
work, like anomaly detection, policy enforcement, and 
blockchain logging, operate as separate services. This 
design allows for flexible growth, improves reliability, and 
supports ongoing updates. Using container technolo­
gies like Docker and orchestration tools like Kubernetes 
allows for flexible resource management. It enhances 
reliability when facing different demands, which is cru­

Abstract: The rapid growth of cloud computing has brought scalability and flexibility to modern organizations, but it has also introduced a new wave of complex and evolving security threats. Traditional security mechanisms, such as static rule-based systems and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), often fall short of identifying advanced attacks like insider threats, privilege escalation, and data breaches. Addressing this gap, we propose SmartTrust, a hybrid deep learning framework designed for real-time threat detection in cloud environments built on Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) principles. SmartTrust integrates CNN, LSTM, and Transformer models to analyze spatial and temporal patterns in network traffic and user behaviours. Unlike conventional models, it leverages Reinforcement Learning to enable adaptive decision-making, allowing it to adjust responses based on real-time contextual signals dynamically. To ensure transparency and tamper-proof event tracking, the framework also incorporates blockchain-based logging that is aligned with ZTA compliance.
